screens.title: Events, Inheritance, and Libraries
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn three practical tools that make smart contracts maintainable and observable. First, events let contracts write structured logs to the transaction receipt so external applications can efficiently monitor activity without expensive on‑chain storage. Second, inheritance, with constructor chaining and method overriding, helps you share logic across related contracts and build clean hierarchies that reduce duplication. Third, libraries provide audited, reusable utility code and the ability to extend types with the using for pattern. Together these features improve gas costs, promote modular design, and enable interoperable contracts. You will see concrete code examples: declaring and emitting a Transfer event, using indexed parameters to filter logs, building a child contract that calls parent constructors and overrides virtual functions, and applying a SafeMath library for safe arithmetic. We will also highlight common pitfalls: indexing limits, forgetting to call parent constructors, unsafe delegatecalls, and library security. By the end you will understand when to emit events, when to inherit, and when to rely on libraries to keep your contracts secure and composable.

screens.title: Bloom Progress Bar
screens.narratorSegment: This mini progress bar maps the learning path. You start by learning the mechanics: how to declare events, how inheritance syntax works, and how library functions are structured. Then you work to understand tradeoffs: when event data should be indexed versus stored, how constructor chaining affects state initialization, and how a library call differs when embedded versus delegatecalled. Next you apply the knowledge through coding: add events to a token contract, write an inheriting contract that overrides a virtual function, and integrate SafeMath with using for to prevent arithmetic errors. Finally, master the ideas by combining them in a small project—an inheritable Pausable token that emits events on state changes and uses a trusted library for arithmetic. Each stage has practical checks: tests that assert events were emitted with indexed parameters, constructor arguments were passed correctly, interfaces were satisfied, and SafeMath prevents overflow. This path makes the theory actionable and focuses your practice on safe patterns you can reuse.

screens.title: Events: declare and emit
screens.narratorSegment: Events are the contract's way to write structured logs that external applications can listen to efficiently. When you declare an event, you define a schema for data you want to record in the transaction log, and when you emit it, that data is appended to the receipt and becomes searchable by index. A practical example is a Transfer event for token movements. Declaring event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 amount) lets UIs filter logs for a user's incoming transfers without scanning all transactions. Importantly, logs are part of the blockchain but are not accessible to other contracts, so events are best for off‑chain indexing and auditing, not for on‑chain logic. One common misconception is to use events as a substitute for persistent state; events are cheaper but ephemeral for contract-to-contract use. Emit events on critical state transitions—value transfers, role changes, or pausing—and use indexed parameters (up to three) to allow quick filtering. As a concrete check, when you emit Transfer on initial minting, a DApp can subscribe to the event and update balances in its UI immediately. Reflect: which state changes here should be persisted and which can be signalled only through events?

keyIdea.text: Use events for efficient off‑chain logs and make frequently filtered fields indexed; do not rely on events for on‑chain logic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Events: declare and emit
Definition

Event declaration and emission

Declare an event with the event keyword and emit it where state changes occur. Indexed parameters make logs searchable by node providers and frontends.

Example declaration
event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 amount);

// Emitting the event
emit Transfer(msg.sender, _recipient, _value);
When to emit

Emit on value transfers, role changes, configuration changes, and other auditable events.

Common mistake

Expecting events to be readable by other contracts. Events are off‑chain artifacts and should not be used for on‑chain control flow.

Concrete scenario

Token transfer logging

A token contract emits Transfer whenever tokens move. A wallet or analytics service filters Transfer by the recipient address to show incoming transactions without scanning all transactions.

Check your understanding
  • Why make fields indexed? — To let providers filter logs efficiently without full scans.
  • How many indexed params? — Up to three; choose the most queryable fields.
Key Takeaway

Use events to provide auditable, searchable history for off‑chain apps. Do not depend on them for on‑chain state.

screens.title: Emitting events and indexed parameters
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete code example that shows how to declare, emit, and then retrieve events from an external consumer. The contract declares event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 value); and emits it at the end of a transfer function. The indexed keywords tell a node to place those fields in topics so you can query for a specific address efficiently. In practice, a dApp connects to a node with a Web3 library and asks for all Transfer events where the recipient equals the user address. This is far cheaper than scanning storage or replaying transactions. One pitfall is assuming events are proof of state; logs reflect what the contract attempted to emit, but a reverted transaction will not include the event. As a concrete example, after deploying the token and calling transfer, open your node or Remix logs to see the emitted Transfer with topics for from and to. When writing tests, assert that the event was emitted with expected indexed values. Consider also indexing at most three parameters and choosing the fields that matter to consumers. Do you see which fields your UI must filter by and which can remain in data?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Emitting events and indexed parameters
Code Walkthrough
// Declaration
event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 value);

// Emitting inside transfer
function _transfer(address sender, address recipient, uint256 amount) internal {
  require(sender != address(0), "ERC20: transfer from the zero address");
  require(recipient != address(0), "ERC20: transfer to the zero address");
  require(_balances[sender] >= amount, "ERC20: transfer amount exceeds balance");

  _balances[sender] = _balances[sender] - amount;
  _balances[recipient] = _balances[recipient] + amount;

  emit Transfer(sender, recipient, amount);
}
Emit check

Events are included in the transaction log only when the transaction succeeds. Tests should assert event emission after successful calls.

Revert pitfall

If the call reverts later, emitted events are discarded. Do not assume events represent committed state until the transaction succeeds.

Retrieval pattern

A dApp uses a Web3 provider to query logs using the event signature and indexed topics. Because indexing is limited to three fields, pick fields that your UI will most often filter by, such as from and to for token transfers.

Example

Subscribe to Transfer where to equals the user's address to show incoming transfers without scanning unrelated events.

Key Takeaway

Emit events for off‑chain consumers and index the fields your applications will query most often.

screens.title: Events vs Storage
screens.narratorSegment: A common design decision is whether to record information in storage or emit it as an event. Storage is persistent and accessible to other contracts and on‑chain code. Events are cheaper and indexed for off‑chain searching, but they cannot be read by contracts. Use storage when the contract logic needs to read or enforce a value later. Use events when you only need an auditable history for off‑chain consumers or logs for analytics. For example, balances must be persisted in storage so transfers and allowances are enforceable. But a history of user‑visible actions, like logging that a user completed a step in a game, can be emitted as an event and consumed by the game frontend. A common mistake is to try to reconstruct contract state solely from events; this is fragile because events reflect past logs and do not provide guarantees for cross-contract reads. When designing, ask: does on‑chain code need this value later? If yes, store it; if no, consider an event. As a quick test, write a small function that both updates state and emits an event; confirm the DApp receives the log while the contract continues to rely on stored state.

keyIdea.text: Store values needed by contract logic; emit events for historical, off‑chain use. Do not try to replace storage with events for on‑chain requirements.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Events vs Storage
Comparison

When to persist vs when to log

Storage
  • Persistent and readable by contracts.
  • Used for balances, allowances, configuration flags.
  • More expensive in gas than logs.
Events
  • Stored in transaction logs and indexed for off‑chain queries.
  • Cheaper than storage and ideal for UIs and analytics.
  • Not readable by on‑chain code, and absent if transaction reverts.
Example

A token contract stores balances but emits Transfer events for wallets. The stored balances are authoritative on‑chain, while events let frontends present a history and react to changes in near real time.

Misconception

Reconstructing state from logs is reliable. In reality logs can be pruned or missed by some providers, so live state must come from contract storage.

Pro Tip

Emit events for audit trails and UI updates, and keep authoritative values in storage for contract logic.

Key Takeaway

Design with the consumer in mind: store what the contract needs; log what outside tools need to see.

screens.title: Inheritance basics with is, virtual, and override
screens.narratorSegment: Inheritance allows a child contract to reuse code and state from parent contracts. In Solidity, you declare inheritance with the is keyword: contract Child is Parent. Members marked public or internal are available to inheriting contracts. When you plan for overriding, mark the parent function virtual and the child implementation override. This explicit pairing reduces accidental shadowing and makes intent clear. Multiple inheritance is allowed but brings ordering concerns: constructor chaining and method resolution follow a linearization rule. A common error is forgetting to call parent constructors that require arguments, which can leave state uninitialized. For example, if TokenBase has a constructor TokenBase(string memory _name, string memory _symbol, uint8 _decimals), the child must call TokenBase(_name, _symbol, _decimals) in its constructor header. Another pitfall is implementing conflicting functions from multiple parents; the child must override and specify the parent implementations it is overriding. As an exercise, create a child contract that inherits TokenBase and AccessControl and explicitly override a sample function using both virtual and override. Ask yourself: which behaviors belong in a shared base and which belong in specific children?

keyIdea.text: Use virtual in parents and override in children, call required parent constructors, and resolve multiple inheritance explicitly to avoid ambiguity.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Inheritance basics
Hierarchy

is, virtual, override

Parents expose behavior and state; children inherit and may override where marked virtual. Explicit override pairs prevent accidental changes.

Pattern
contract Parent {
  function greet() public virtual returns (string memory) {
    return "hello";
  }
}

contract Child is Parent {
  function greet() public override returns (string memory) {
    return "hello from child";
  }
}
Constructor chaining

If a parent expects constructor arguments, the child must call it in its constructor header. This ensures parent state is initialized predictably and avoids uninitialized variables that can lead to security issues.

Example

constructor(string memory _name) Parent(_name) { ... } will pass arguments to the Parent constructor and initialize its state.

Common mistake

Forgetting to call a required parent constructor leaves the parent state defaulted and can break invariants. Always check parent constructors when inheriting.

Key Takeaway

Make inheritance explicit: mark overridable functions and call parent constructors with required arguments to maintain invariants.

screens.title: Multiple inheritance and method resolution
screens.narratorSegment: When a contract inherits from multiple parents, Solidity computes a deterministic order for resolving which parent implementation applies. This is called linearization. The order affects constructor invocation and which implementation a child sees when multiple parents define the same function. The safe practice is to design minimal overlapping behavior or explicitly override ambiguous functions in the child and list the parent contracts in the correct order. For example, if MyToken is TokenBase, AccessControl, IERC20, and two parents both implement a function with the same signature, you must provide an override in MyToken and call the specific parent implementations if needed. Constructor chaining also follows the linearization order, so pass arguments in the child constructor header to each parent as required. A misconception is assuming the order listed is unimportant; in reality it determines which base constructors run first. As an exercise, list parent contracts from the most derived to the most base in the child declaration and implement any required overrides, explicitly calling parent functions when you need aggregated behavior. This prevents accidental shadowing and makes class relationships clear to reviewers and auditors.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Multiple inheritance
Process

Resolve conflicts and call parent constructors

Rule of thumb
  • List parents from most derived to most base.
  • Override functions with ambiguous signatures in the child.
  • Explicitly call parent constructors with required args.
Example override
contract A { function foo() public virtual returns (string memory) { return "A"; } }
contract B { function foo() public virtual returns (string memory) { return "B"; } }
contract C is A, B {
  function foo() public override(A, B) returns (string memory) {
    return B.foo(); // explicit resolution
  }
}
Checklist

Before deploying, verify parent constructor calls, explicit overrides exist for overlapping functions, and unit tests cover inherited behavior across the hierarchy.

screens.title: Abstract contracts vs Interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: Abstract contracts and interfaces both describe expected behavior, but they serve different purposes. An abstract contract can include implemented functions, state variables, and constructors while also leaving at least one function without an implementation. It acts as a partial base that child contracts can extend. An interface is stricter: it can only declare function signatures and events, with no state or constructors. Use an abstract contract when you want to provide shared logic or storage and leave specific functions to be implemented by children. Use an interface when you want to define a standard contract of behavior that multiple implementations must follow, like an ERC standard. A misconception is to treat interfaces as interchangeable with abstract contracts; interfaces cannot hold state or helper functions. When interacting with external contracts, prefer interfaces to declare the minimal surface you need. As a concrete example, IERC20 defines function signatures and events so any token implementation can be discovered and used without knowing its internals. Ask yourself: do I need shared stored state or only a behavioral contract? That choice decides abstract contract or interface.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Abstract contracts vs Interfaces
Abstract Contract

Can have implemented functions, state variables, and constructors. Declare it when you want shared behavior and partial implementations for child contracts to extend.

Example
abstract contract AccessControl {
  address public owner;
  constructor() { owner = msg.sender; }
  function _authorize(address user) internal virtual returns (bool);
}
Interface

Only function signatures and events. No state, no constructors. Use when you need a strict contract that other implementations must follow.

Example
interface IERC20 {
  event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 value);
  function totalSupply() external view returns (uint256);
  function transfer(address recipient, uint256 amount) external returns (bool);
}
Key Takeaway

Use interfaces for interoperability and abstract contracts when you want to supply shared logic or storage to children.

screens.title: Libraries and the using for pattern
screens.narratorSegment: Libraries are stateless containers of reusable functions. Internal library functions are embedded at compile time into the calling contract, which saves gas and avoids external calls. Public or external library functions are executed via delegatecall in the context of the caller, which allows the library to operate on the caller's storage but also introduces security considerations. Use libraries for utility math, complex data structures, or to extend types with using for. For example, using SafeMath for uint256 lets you call myUint. add(other) and ensures checks like preventing overflow. The SafeMath add function performs the addition, checks the result is at least the original value, and reverts on overflow. A critical risk is an untrusted library performing unsafe delegatecalls; only use audited libraries for public functions. When integrating, prefer internal functions where possible, and if you must rely on a deployed library address, ensure it is immutable and audited. As a concrete illustration, review the SafeMath add and sub functions and consider testing arithmetic boundaries in your unit tests. Ask: can this code be embedded as internal to avoid delegatecall risks?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Libraries and using for
Library Example
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
library SafeMath {
  function add(uint256 a, uint256 b) internal pure returns (uint256) {
    uint256 c = a + b;
    require(c >= a, "SafeMath: addition overflow");
    return c;
  }

  function sub(uint256 a, uint256 b) internal pure returns (uint256) {
    require(b <= a, "SafeMath: subtraction underflow");
    uint256 c = a - b;
    return c;
  }
}

// Usage
using SafeMath for uint256;
uint256 x = a.add(b);
Internal functions are inlined; public functions incur delegatecall. Prefer internal embedding for core utilities and audited deployed libraries for shared, upgradable code only when necessary.
Security considerations
  • Delegatecall runs library code in the caller's storage context—audited libraries only.
  • Embedding internal functions avoids runtime external dependencies.
  • Test edge cases like underflow/overflow and unusual input sizes.
Pro Tip

Use using for to make calls expressive and readable, and prefer internal functions so behavior is compiled into the contract where possible.

Key Takeaway

Libraries save gas and centralize trusted logic. Choose internal embeds for safety and audit public libraries before using their addresses.

keyIdea.title: Activity goal
keyIdea.text: Implement IPausable, Pausable, and MyPausableToken; emit Paused/Unpaused events and enforce pause checks in functions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Pausable activity
Files to create
IPausable.sol (interface)
// IPausable.sol
interface IPausable {
  event Paused(address account);
  event Unpaused(address account);

  function paused() external view returns (bool);
  function pause() external;
  function unpause() external;
}
Pausable.sol (abstract)
// Pausable.sol
abstract contract Pausable is IPausable {
  bool private _paused;
  constructor(){ _paused = false; }
  function paused() public view virtual override returns (bool) { return _paused; }

  modifier whenNotPaused(){ require(!_paused, "Pausable: paused"); _; }
  modifier whenPaused(){ require(_paused, "Pausable: not paused"); _; }

  function _pause() internal virtual { require(!_paused, "Pausable: already paused"); _paused = true; emit Paused(msg.sender); }
  function _unpause() internal virtual { require(_paused, "Pausable: not paused"); _paused = false; emit Unpaused(msg.sender); }

  function pause() public virtual override {}
  function unpause() public virtual override {}
}
MyPausableToken.sol (implementation)
// MyPausableToken.sol
contract MyPausableToken is Pausable {
  address public owner;
  event ImportantActionDone(address indexed by, uint256 timestamp);

  modifier onlyOwner(){ require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can call this function"); _; }

  constructor(){ owner = msg.sender; }

  function pause() public override onlyOwner { _pause(); }
  function unpause() public override onlyOwner { _unpause(); }

  function doSomethingImportant() public whenNotPaused {
    emit ImportantActionDone(msg.sender, block.timestamp);
  }

  function getContractBalance() public view returns (uint256) {
    return address(this).balance;
  }
}
Verification steps
  1. Deploy MyPausableToken and call pause; observe Paused emitted.
  2. Call doSomethingImportant while paused and confirm it reverts.
  3. Unpause and call doSomethingImportant; confirm ImportantActionDone event.
Key Takeaway

This activity demonstrates how interfaces define the contract, abstract contracts provide partial implementations and events, and children implement ownership and expose safe, audited behavior.

If the answer is yes, you are following safer patterns.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn three practical tools that make smart contracts maintainable and observable. First, events let contracts write structured logs to the transaction receipt so external applications can efficiently monitor activity without expensive on‑chain storage. Second, inheritance, with constructor chaining and method overriding, helps you share logic across related contracts and build clean hierarchies that reduce duplication. Third, libraries provide audited, reusable utility code and the ability to extend types with the using for pattern. Together these features improve gas costs, promote modular design, and enable interoperable contracts. You will see concrete code examples: declaring and emitting a Transfer event, using indexed parameters to filter logs, building a child contract that calls parent constructors and overrides virtual functions, and applying a SafeMath library for safe arithmetic. We will also highlight common pitfalls: indexing limits, forgetting to call parent constructors, unsafe delegatecalls, and library security. By the end you will understand when to emit events, when to inherit, and when to rely on libraries to keep your contracts secure and composable.

These objectives focus on observable behavior, reusable structure, and audited utilities. First, you'll declare and emit events so external tools can react to contract activity. You'll learn how indexed parameters make filtering efficient and when to avoid storing transient data on-chain. Second, you'll implement inheritance using the is keyword, including constructor chaining and method overriding. This teaches you to share state and behavior safely while avoiding common linearization mistakes. Third, you'll differentiate between abstract contracts and interfaces. You will know when to use partial implementations and when to enforce a strict blueprint without state. Fourth, you'll integrate Solidity libraries and use the using for directive to extend primitive types and centralize vetted logic. Each objective includes a verification milestone so you can confirm competency: emitting correct events in a demo, writing a child contract that calls parent constructors, implementing an interface, and applying a SafeMath library call. These are practical skills you will use immediately when building tokens, access control, and reusable utilities.

This mini progress bar maps the learning path. You start by learning the mechanics: how to declare events, how inheritance syntax works, and how library functions are structured. Then you work to understand tradeoffs: when event data should be indexed versus stored, how constructor chaining affects state initialization, and how a library call differs when embedded versus delegatecalled. Next you apply the knowledge through coding: add events to a token contract, write an inheriting contract that overrides a virtual function, and integrate SafeMath with using for to prevent arithmetic errors. Finally, master the ideas by combining them in a small project—an inheritable Pausable token that emits events on state changes and uses a trusted library for arithmetic. Each stage has practical checks: tests that assert events were emitted with indexed parameters, constructor arguments were passed correctly, interfaces were satisfied, and SafeMath prevents overflow. This path makes the theory actionable and focuses your practice on safe patterns you can reuse.

Events are the contract's way to write structured logs that external applications can listen to efficiently. When you declare an event, you define a schema for data you want to record in the transaction log, and when you emit it, that data is appended to the receipt and becomes searchable by index. A practical example is a Transfer event for token movements. Declaring event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 amount) lets UIs filter logs for a user's incoming transfers without scanning all transactions. Importantly, logs are part of the blockchain but are not accessible to other contracts, so events are best for off‑chain indexing and auditing, not for on‑chain logic. One common misconception is to use events as a substitute for persistent state; events are cheaper but ephemeral for contract-to-contract use. Emit events on critical state transitions—value transfers, role changes, or pausing—and use indexed parameters (up to three) to allow quick filtering. As a concrete check, when you emit Transfer on initial minting, a DApp can subscribe to the event and update balances in its UI immediately. Reflect: which state changes here should be persisted and which can be signalled only through events?

Let's walk through a concrete code example that shows how to declare, emit, and then retrieve events from an external consumer. The contract declares event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 value); and emits it at the end of a transfer function. The indexed keywords tell a node to place those fields in topics so you can query for a specific address efficiently. In practice, a dApp connects to a node with a Web3 library and asks for all Transfer events where the recipient equals the user address. This is far cheaper than scanning storage or replaying transactions. One pitfall is assuming events are proof of state; logs reflect what the contract attempted to emit, but a reverted transaction will not include the event. As a concrete example, after deploying the token and calling transfer, open your node or Remix logs to see the emitted Transfer with topics for from and to. When writing tests, assert that the event was emitted with expected indexed values. Consider also indexing at most three parameters and choosing the fields that matter to consumers. Do you see which fields your UI must filter by and which can remain in data?

A common design decision is whether to record information in storage or emit it as an event. Storage is persistent and accessible to other contracts and on‑chain code. Events are cheaper and indexed for off‑chain searching, but they cannot be read by contracts. Use storage when the contract logic needs to read or enforce a value later. Use events when you only need an auditable history for off‑chain consumers or logs for analytics. For example, balances must be persisted in storage so transfers and allowances are enforceable. But a history of user‑visible actions, like logging that a user completed a step in a game, can be emitted as an event and consumed by the game frontend. A common mistake is to try to reconstruct contract state solely from events; this is fragile because events reflect past logs and do not provide guarantees for cross-contract reads. When designing, ask: does on‑chain code need this value later? If yes, store it; if no, consider an event. As a quick test, write a small function that both updates state and emits an event; confirm the DApp receives the log while the contract continues to rely on stored state.

Inheritance allows a child contract to reuse code and state from parent contracts. In Solidity, you declare inheritance with the is keyword: contract Child is Parent. Members marked public or internal are available to inheriting contracts. When you plan for overriding, mark the parent function virtual and the child implementation override. This explicit pairing reduces accidental shadowing and makes intent clear. Multiple inheritance is allowed but brings ordering concerns: constructor chaining and method resolution follow a linearization rule. A common error is forgetting to call parent constructors that require arguments, which can leave state uninitialized. For example, if TokenBase has a constructor TokenBase(string memory _name, string memory _symbol, uint8 _decimals), the child must call TokenBase(_name, _symbol, _decimals) in its constructor header. Another pitfall is implementing conflicting functions from multiple parents; the child must override and specify the parent implementations it is overriding. As an exercise, create a child contract that inherits TokenBase and AccessControl and explicitly override a sample function using both virtual and override. Ask yourself: which behaviors belong in a shared base and which belong in specific children?

When a contract inherits from multiple parents, Solidity computes a deterministic order for resolving which parent implementation applies. This is called linearization. The order affects constructor invocation and which implementation a child sees when multiple parents define the same function. The safe practice is to design minimal overlapping behavior or explicitly override ambiguous functions in the child and list the parent contracts in the correct order. For example, if MyToken is TokenBase, AccessControl, IERC20, and two parents both implement a function with the same signature, you must provide an override in MyToken and call the specific parent implementations if needed. Constructor chaining also follows the linearization order, so pass arguments in the child constructor header to each parent as required. A misconception is assuming the order listed is unimportant; in reality it determines which base constructors run first. As an exercise, list parent contracts from the most derived to the most base in the child declaration and implement any required overrides, explicitly calling parent functions when you need aggregated behavior. This prevents accidental shadowing and makes class relationships clear to reviewers and auditors.

Abstract contracts and interfaces both describe expected behavior, but they serve different purposes. An abstract contract can include implemented functions, state variables, and constructors while also leaving at least one function without an implementation. It acts as a partial base that child contracts can extend. An interface is stricter: it can only declare function signatures and events, with no state or constructors. Use an abstract contract when you want to provide shared logic or storage and leave specific functions to be implemented by children. Use an interface when you want to define a standard contract of behavior that multiple implementations must follow, like an ERC standard. A misconception is to treat interfaces as interchangeable with abstract contracts; interfaces cannot hold state or helper functions. When interacting with external contracts, prefer interfaces to declare the minimal surface you need. As a concrete example, IERC20 defines function signatures and events so any token implementation can be discovered and used without knowing its internals. Ask yourself: do I need shared stored state or only a behavioral contract? That choice decides abstract contract or interface.

Libraries are stateless containers of reusable functions. Internal library functions are embedded at compile time into the calling contract, which saves gas and avoids external calls. Public or external library functions are executed via delegatecall in the context of the caller, which allows the library to operate on the caller's storage but also introduces security considerations. Use libraries for utility math, complex data structures, or to extend types with using for. For example, using SafeMath for uint256 lets you call myUint. add(other) and ensures checks like preventing overflow. The SafeMath add function performs the addition, checks the result is at least the original value, and reverts on overflow. A critical risk is an untrusted library performing unsafe delegatecalls; only use audited libraries for public functions. When integrating, prefer internal functions where possible, and if you must rely on a deployed library address, ensure it is immutable and audited. As a concrete illustration, review the SafeMath add and sub functions and consider testing arithmetic boundaries in your unit tests. Ask: can this code be embedded as internal to avoid delegatecall risks?

This exercise validates both your understanding and practical skills.

Let's summarize the essential ideas to carry forward. Events are the primary mechanism to log structured data for off‑chain consumers; mark frequently queried fields indexed up to three parameters and use events to provide auditable histories. Inheritance enables code reuse; parents expose public and internal members and children use is to inherit. Use virtual and override to manage method substitution and always call parent constructors when they require arguments. Third, use libraries for utility code and prefer internal functions to embed code at compile time; if you rely on deployed libraries with public functions, ensure they are audited because delegatecall executes in your storage context. These rules make contracts easier to audit, cheaper to run, and more interoperable with other systems. If the answer is yes, you are following safer patterns.
